experiences.reading: At morning break, Sione bounced a basketball beside the court. Boom, boom, bounce. Levi tapped his shoes to the beat. Aroha called, “Ball, wall, tall!” The words sounded alike at the end. “That's rhyme,” she said. Sione tried a poem: “The ball goes high. It reaches the sky.” He liked the matching sounds, but the poem did not tell the whole story. He added a line about his friend missing the hoop and everyone laughing. When he read it aloud, the new line felt too long. He cut out three words. Now the beat was easier to follow. His teacher explained that rhythm is the pattern of sounds and stresses in words. Rhyme happens when words share ending sounds. A poem can have rhythm without rhyme. Sione tried clapping as he read. He changed one word so the line matched his claps. The finished poem sounded like a quick game. Sione decided to call it “Break-Time Bounce.”  Levi asked if the poem needed the words “ball” and “wall” in every line. Sione said no. He wanted the words to sound good and make sense. They clapped the ending together before running back to play.

experiences.reading: Mele heard a familiar rhythm each afternoon as she walked home. A gate clicked. A dog barked twice. A bus stopped with a long hiss. Children called across the road. She decided to turn the sounds into a poem. Her first version rhymed every pair of lines, but she had to use awkward words to make the endings match. Her cousin read it and asked why a dog was described as a “royal frog”. Mele laughed. She had chosen “frog” only because it rhymed with “dog”. She rewrote the verse, keeping the sound pattern but using words that made sense. “The gate clicks shut. Two paws race by. A bus sighs under the evening sky.” Some lines rhymed; others did not. Mele clapped while reading and noticed that the short line about the gate sounded sharp, while the longer bus line slowed the pace. She understood that rhythm could suggest movement and mood. She chose not to force another rhyme into the ending. Instead, she repeated “home” twice to show where the sounds were leading her. Her final poem felt like her own street, not a collection of words chosen only for their endings.  Her teacher asked the class to tap the beat of two versions. Students could keep time with the shorter opening, but they slowed down during the bus line. Mele said that was exactly what she wanted: the walk home was busy at first, then calmer near her gate. The repeated word “home” made the ending feel settled rather than rushed.

experiences.reading: Jayden practised a short poem before rugby training. He wanted the opening to sound energetic, so he used brief phrases: “Run. Turn. Pass. Go.” Each word landed like a footstep. Then he wrote a longer line about waiting for the whistle. When he performed the poem, the change in pace made his teammates look up. His teacher had explained that rhythm came from stressed syllables, pauses and repeated patterns, not just rhyming endings. Jayden experimented with three versions. In the first, every line rhymed, but the message felt predictable. In the second, the lines were all the same length and sounded flat. In the third, he used short lines for action and a deliberate pause before the final whistle. He added the internal rhyme “fast past the last defender”, but removed another rhyme that distracted from the play. One teammate said the pause felt like the moment before a kick. Jayden realised that sound could imitate experience. The poem's rhythm was not merely a beat to keep listeners entertained; it shaped how they felt time passing. He revised the final stanza to slow down after the game, when the players were tired and the field became quiet. The contrast made the earlier speed more noticeable.  At training, Jayden asked a teammate to read the poem without seeing his performance notes. The teammate rushed the waiting line, so Jayden added a line break before “whistle”. He learned that the printed page could suggest a pause even when he was not there to perform it. He kept the repeated action verbs because their hard sounds suited the quick movement of the game.  He compared the sound of the opening with the end by tapping each line on his knee. The first stanza had quick stresses; the final stanza stretched its vowels and included more pauses. The contrast helped listeners hear the shift from effort to rest. He decided not to add a rhyme simply because one was available.

experiences.reading: Jayden sat in a hospital waiting room while his aunt received treatment. A clock ticked above the reception desk. Shoes moved quietly along the corridor. Every few minutes, a trolley rattled past. He tried to write a poem, but his first lines all ended in cheerful rhymes. They sounded wrong for the room. He crossed them out and listened to the clock again. “Tick. Wait. Tick.” The short words seemed to make time move slowly. He followed them with a longer sentence about the bright corridor stretching beyond the doors. The shift in rhythm reflected how waiting could feel both still and endless. When his aunt returned with reassuring news, Jayden wanted the poem to change. He used a smoother sequence of sounds and a line that flowed without interruption. His teacher later explained that a poet's rhythm could follow emotional movement. Rhyme might create expectation, but it could also sound forced or inappropriate if it conflicted with the subject. Jayden considered adding a perfect rhyme to the final line. Instead, he repeated the word “breath”. The repetition linked the tense beginning to the calmer ending. A classmate noticed that the poem did not describe every medical detail. It focused on the experience of waiting. Jayden felt that was right. The pauses and changing pace communicated what a factual report could not.  Later Jayden noticed that he had written three long sentences in the middle of the poem. They made the waiting feel endless, but one contained an unnecessary detail about a poster on the wall. He removed that detail while keeping the longer rhythm. He also tried the poem with no punctuation and found that the emotional turn became unclear. A full stop before the news helped the reader sense a change. He kept the final repetition because it echoed the earlier anxiety without repeating the same feeling.  The teacher invited students to explain how the poem might sound if every line had the same number of beats. Jayden imagined a steady march, which would make the uncertainty seem controlled. His actual poem needed uneven timing because waiting had felt unpredictable. He noticed that the phrase “Tick. Wait. Tick.” also created a pattern that readers could anticipate. Breaking it later made the reassuring news feel like a genuine interruption. When his aunt read the poem, she said the repeated word “breath” captured the relief more clearly than a sentence stating that everyone was happy. Jayden understood that a sound pattern could carry an emotional argument.

experiences.reading: Mele listened to an old radio recording of a spoken-word performance. The speaker began with a regular beat, then stopped unexpectedly before one important word. The silence drew more attention than a louder voice might have done. Mele wanted to understand why. She marked the stressed syllables in the opening lines and noticed that the pattern made the audience expect a continuation. Breaking the pattern created tension. She experimented with a poem about receiving difficult news. Her first draft used end rhyme in every line. Although the sounds were neat, the predictable pattern made the subject feel strangely light. She removed several rhymes and kept a repeated phrase: “I waited.” Each repetition had a different number of words after it. The phrase became a measure of time rather than a decorative refrain. She then placed a single-word line after a long sentence. Reading it aloud, she noticed how the sudden stop changed her breathing. Her teacher asked whether that effect would remain for a reader who never heard the poem performed. Mele examined the page. Line breaks and punctuation provided visual clues, but they could not control every reader's pace. She added a dash where the pause mattered most and removed one unnecessary comma. A classmate read the poem with a different emphasis and created a slightly different meaning. Mele accepted that rhythm was partly shaped by the reader. They discussed how musicality, repetition, stress and silence could influence interpretation without determining it completely. Mele also compared the sound of her poem with a prose account of the same event. The prose conveyed the sequence efficiently; the poem made the waiting feel prolonged. By the final draft, she understood that rhythm was not simply an ornament or a requirement to rhyme. It was a method of organising emotional experience in time.  For the workshop presentation, Mele asked two classmates to perform the same stanza. One paused after “waited”; the other stressed the final word. Their readings suggested different degrees of resignation. Mele revised the punctuation to make her preferred emphasis more likely, while recognising she could not dictate every performance. She also tested the poem with a quiet spoken delivery rather than an exaggerated dramatic voice. The quieter version made the repeated phrase sound more personal. She concluded that performance choices were part of the poem's interpretation, not an optional layer added after writing.  Mele questioned whether repeated words always strengthened a poem. She found that using “I waited” too often made the refrain lose force. She removed one repetition and left a space where listeners expected it. The absence created its own emphasis. She also tried ending the poem with a neat couplet, but the perfect rhyme suggested an emotional resolution that the experience did not offer. She kept an unrhymed ending. Her teacher observed that deliberate irregularity could be as controlled as a regular beat, provided the writer understood its effect. Mele annotated the final draft with performance choices: slow at the opening, restrained through the middle, and a longer silence after the last line. Those decisions connected the poem's form to its meaning.  At the end, Mele compared the recording with her written poem once more. The recording allowed the performer to control the silence directly, while the page relied on lineation and punctuation to invite a pause. She did not rank one medium above the other. Instead, she revised each for its audience. She also noticed that a listener could hear hesitation in the voice, while a reader might infer it from a broken line. Both experiences depended on rhythm, but they offered different kinds of evidence. That distinction helped her prepare a performance that respected the written poem without simply repeating it mechanically.
